tldr: This study shows that by self-distilling successful action chunks from the execution logs of test-time compute (TTC)—which scores and aggregates multiple candidates at inference time—directly into LoRA parameters, a model can retain about 74% of the TTC performance gain even during verifier-free single-candidate generation, while subsequent TTC further improves overall performance.
hero_caption: An overview of the proposed framework, "Verify, Act, Distill." During inference, test-time compute (TTC) executes a weighted aggregate of multiple action candidates scored by a verifier. Successful action chunks are then distilled directly into LoRA parameters via supervised flow matching, enabling model adaptation without any additional reinforcement learning.
overview:
In vision-language-action (VLA) models for robotics, test-time compute (TTC)—generating multiple action candidates at inference time and selecting the best one with a verifier—has attracted significant attention as an effective way to boost performance. However, conventional TTC leaves model parameters frozen during inference. No matter how smart its decisions are in the field, the model itself never becomes any smarter. In other words, every time it repeats the same task, it must generate and score candidates from scratch all over again, wasting computational resources.

The authors asked a simple question: "Aren't the actions evaluated and executed at inference time already the highest-quality supervision data available?" In the proposed framework, "Verify, Act, Distill," the robot executes actions weighted and aggregated by a fixed verifier. The action chunks from as few as 10 successful episodes are then directly distilled into the VLA model's LoRA parameters using standard flow-matching loss. It requires no additional reinforcement learning (RL) loops and no separate teacher model.

Evaluating across the 40 tasks of the LIBERO benchmark, lightweight single-candidate inference without a verifier retained about 74% of the performance improvement obtained by aggregating eight candidates (Agg-8). Furthermore, applying TTC again to the distilled model led to a "re-amplification" effect with even higher success rates. This paper neatly demonstrates that inference-time compute does not have to be a disposable, one-off cost, but can be funneled into permanent adaptation for the model itself.
contributions: Proposed a concise adaptation framework that directly distills verified action chunks from TTC execution into LoRA parameters without additional RL or teacher rollout generation
Demonstrated that distilling just 10 successful episodes consolidates about 74% of the performance gains of TTC into verifier-free, single-candidate generation
Proved a synergistic effect where distillation raises the candidate generation quality of the base policy, enabling subsequent TTC executions to achieve even higher performance (re-amplification)
Provided detailed analyses regarding the necessity of a success filter, teacher data chunking methods, and behavioral limits under distribution shifts (LIBERO-plus)

sections.heading: Turning One-Off Inference Compute into Model Learning
sections.summary: While test-time compute (TTC) that evaluates multiple candidates is powerful, it repeatedly wastes computation because the policy remains frozen. This paper distills successful aggregated actions from TTC directly into the VLA, raising baseline single-candidate generation performance while re-amplifying the benefits of subsequent TTC.
sections.details:
Generative VLA models based on diffusion or flow matching can produce diverse action chunks from the same observation. Recently, test-time compute (TTC)—generating multiple action candidates at inference time and scoring them with a pre-trained verifier—has been shown to significantly boost robot success rates.

However, existing TTC methods share a major drawback: they do not update the base policy weights at all. Even when the system makes good decisions during execution, no feedback remains in the model parameters. As long as it operates in the same environment, it must repeatedly burn heavy computational resources generating and evaluating candidates. This is highly inefficient for real-world deployments.

The key insight here is that the process of evaluating candidates and selecting good actions during inference produces extremely high-quality supervision data. If those actions can be fed back into the model itself, the robot should maintain high success rates even during fast single-candidate ($N=1$) inference without a verifier. Furthermore, if the adapted model generates higher-quality candidates right from the start, a virtuous cycle can emerge where subsequent TTC pushes the performance ceiling even higher (re-amplification).

The proposed framework, "Verify, Act, Distill," realizes this cycle in a surprisingly simple way. Without training an RL expert or optimizing actions via critic gradients, it collects aggregated chunks from successful rollouts and updates LoRA parameters using standard flow-matching loss. With just 10 adaptation episodes, it substantially raises single-candidate inference success rates.

sections.heading: The Intersection of Test-Time Search and Post-Deployment Adaptation
sections.summary: While test-time improvement via candidate selection (TTC) and post-deployment RL adaptation are widely studied, most methods freeze verifiers or introduce complex architectures. This work occupies a unique position by directly distilling the everyday execution results of a fixed verifier into the generative VLA.
sections.details:
To understand where this work stands, let's look at the surrounding literature.

### Inference-Time Improvements via Candidate Evaluation
Approaches that spend compute at test time include V-GPS, which reranks candidates using a value function, RoboMonkey, which pairs policies with verifiers, and RoVer, which uses reward models. However, all of these are confined to the choice of which candidate to execute; none funnel the selection back into the model's own weights.

### Guiding Generation and Lookahead Search
An increasing number of studies invest compute directly into the generative process through noise optimization, Q-function-guided flows, or tree search with world models. For example, SVA distills search results into a Q-evaluator, but leaves the VLA itself frozen. In contrast, this paper differs fundamentally by distilling improved actions directly into the VLA.

### Post-Deployment Adaptation and Reinforcement Learning (RL)
For post-deployment adaptation of VLAs, methods such as DSRL (adjusting noise space with RL), TT-VLA (updating LoRA via environmental feedback), and PPO-based policy optimization (e.g., VLA-RL) are common. Others, like PA-RL and PLD, distill improved actions. However, PA-RL requires additional local optimization via a critic, and PLD relies on an auxiliary RL expert (a residual policy). This study elegantly reuses aggregated actions naturally obtained during standard TTC execution as supervision data, requiring no extra RL loops or auxiliary models.

sections.heading: Verify, Act, Distill: A Surprisingly Simple Adaptation Mechanism
sections.summary: The policy executes a weighted average of multiple candidates (Agg-N) using a fixed verifier and stores the action chunks of successful runs into a buffer. Fine-tuning LoRA weights for just 200 steps using standard flow-matching loss completes the adaptation.
sections.details:
The framework workflow is straightforward, consisting of three stages: inference, execution, and updating.

### 3.1 Problem Setting
Given observation $o_t$ (images from two cameras, an 8-dimensional proprioceptive state, and a language instruction), the VLA model $\pi_{\theta_0}$ (SmolVLA is used here) generates a normalized action chunk of $H_1=50$ steps starting from initial noise $z$. At each replanning interval, only the first $H_2=10$ steps are executed in the environment. During the adaptation phase, the robot runs $K$ episodes per task (defaulting to just 10) and uses only successful ones to update LoRA parameters. Adaptation is performed independently for each task without transferring knowledge across tasks.

### 3.2 Verify and Act: Candidate Aggregation via a Fixed Verifier
At each replanning step, $N$ candidate chunks (typically 8) are generated. The first is drawn from a standard normal distribution, while the remaining seven are generated with slightly broader variance ($\alpha=1.2$) to ensure diversity.
The verifier $V_{\text{act}}$ is a 6-layer Transformer that takes observation features and the first $H_2=10$ steps of candidate actions as input and outputs a scalar score $s_i$. It is pre-trained offline with Bradley-Terry loss so that candidates closer to ground-truth actions in successful trajectories receive higher scores.
Instead of picking the single highest-scoring candidate (argmax), the system executes a weighted average (Agg-8) based on softmax weights with a temperature parameter $\lambda=0.3$. This produces an execution plan $\bar{A}$ that is smoother and more reliable than any individual candidate.

### 3.3 Distill: Supervised Updates from Successful Rollouts
This is the core essence of the approach. Only when an episode succeeds are the aggregated action chunks $\bar{A}$ saved into a buffer as training data. Data from failed episodes is discarded (success filtering).
Using this data, only the LoRA parameters (rank 8, just 0.37M trainable parameters) inserted into the base model's action expert are updated with standard flow-matching loss for 200 steps.
Notably, while only the first 10 steps ($H_2$) were executed in the environment, the entire 50-step plan ($H_1$) is used as supervision. This preserves the exact input/output format and objective function from SmolVLA's pre-training, enabling efficient learning across the entire coherent action plan.

captions.F1: The overall workflow of the method. On the left, candidate actions are aggregated with verifier weights and executed (Act). On the right, full planned chunks from successful episodes are collected in a buffer and distilled into LoRA parameters via flow matching (Distill).

sections.heading: Distilling Just 10 Episodes Consolidates and Re-Amplifies TTC Gains
sections.summary: Across 40 LIBERO tasks, distilling 10 episodes boosted single-candidate success rates without a verifier from 54.1% to 70.6%. Applying TTC again to the distilled model reached 82.3%, with clear single-candidate improvements confirmed even under distribution shifts.
sections.details:
Experiments were conducted on all four suites of the LIBERO benchmark (Spatial, Object, Goal, and Long, totaling 40 tasks). The primary model used was SmolVLA trained for 5k steps (base success rate 54.1%), representing a checkpoint with room for adaptation.

### 4.2 Main Results: Retaining Gains and Re-Amplifying TTC
- **Consolidating ~74% of TTC gains**: Aggregating eight candidates (Agg-8) improved the base policy's success rate from 54.1% to 76.4%. Distilling from these Agg-8 successes yielded a policy that achieved a **70.6%** success rate during verifier-free single-candidate ($N=1$) inference. Roughly 74% of the performance boost provided by TTC was firmly retained in the model parameters (improving on 34 out of 40 tasks).
- **Re-amplification of subsequent TTC**: Applying Agg-8 again using this distilled policy further pushed the success rate to **82.3%**. A particularly large jump was recorded on the challenging "LIBERO-Long" suite requiring long-horizon planning, leaping from 44.0% to 57.8%.
- **Outperforming simple self-imitation**: The method significantly outperformed the "Self" baseline (63.7%), which imitates the base model's own successful rollouts without a verifier. This highlights that supervising with high-quality aggregated actions from a verifier is crucial.
- **Substantial edge over noise-space RL (GRPO)**: Compared to N-GRPO (58.1% / 79.2%), which optimizes noise space via RL using verifier scores as rewards under the same 10-episode budget, directly distilling actions demonstrated overwhelmingly superior sample efficiency.

### 4.3–4.6 Ablations and Analyses
- **Behavior on a mature checkpoint (10k)**: On a 10k checkpoint (base 83.2%), distilled single-candidate inference improved to 86.2%. However, running Agg-8 again yielded 89.8% (compared to 90.4% originally), showing no re-amplification. As candidate differences become minute, the fixed verifier's discriminative resolution likely falls short.
- **Importance of the success filter**: Distilling failed episodes along with successes dropped the success rate to 64.4%. Filtering out failed executions is essential.
- **Distribution shifts (LIBERO-plus)**: Under unseen perturbations, single-candidate inference still showed a solid +3.9 percentage point improvement. However, in 66 out of 140 tasks, the model failed all 10 adaptation trials, highlighting a limitation where adaptation cannot even begin.
- **Candidate count and adaptation budget**: Across inference candidate counts from $N=1$ to $16$, the distilled model consistently outperformed the base model. Furthermore, noticeable gains were achieved with budgets as small as $K=2$ or $5$ episodes, corroborating the framework's data efficiency.

The left plot compares the base and distilled models (verifier-free, single-candidate), where most points (34 tasks) lie above the diagonal, showing clear gains. The right plot compares Agg-8 performance, showing that distillation pushes the TTC ceiling even higher.

The distilled model (orange) consistently outperforms the base model across candidate counts, showing significant improvements with just a few adaptation episodes.

sections.heading: Conclusions and Challenges for Real-World Deployment
sections.summary: This work turns TTC from a one-time execution selector into an adaptation signal for the model. However, real-world deployment faces challenges, including reliance on verifier discrimination, the requirement of at least one success, and performance regressions on select tasks.
sections.details:
"Verify, Act, Distill" converts test-time computational costs from disposable overhead into a data-generation engine that makes future inference lighter and smarter. This eliminates the need to run heavy verifiers continuously to maintain high-precision control.

At the same time, the paper openly addresses several limitations and prerequisites for practical application:
- **Dependence on verifier quality**: The framework assumes that the pre-trained verifier can accurately judge action quality. Training the verifier requires offline demonstration trajectories; it cannot supply proper supervision in completely unfamiliar scenarios.
- **The "at least one success" requirement**: Because it relies on a success filter, adaptation cannot start if an agent fails all 10 trials, such as under severe distribution shifts. In real-robot setups, the reliability of automated success detection is also a concern.
- **Lack of regression safeguards**: Performance gains are not unconditional across every task; success rates degraded on 5 out of 40 tasks. Safety mechanisms such as fallback to the base policy or verification checkpoints will be necessary.

sections.heading: Appendix: World-Model Features and Improvement Vector Analysis
sections.summary: The appendix explores using world-model latent predictions in verifiers (V_latent), ablates unexecuted action supervision, and analyzes geometric reasons why TTC re-amplification diminishes on highly trained models.
sections.details:
The appendix provides several interesting supplementary experiments that deepen our understanding of the framework.

### Is supervision for unexecuted steps necessary? (Appendix B.1)
While the main method executes only the first 10 steps ($H_2$) but distills all 50 steps ($H_1$), an ablation masked the loss to only the executed 10 steps. Surprisingly, restricting loss to those 10 steps increased the average success rate from 70.6% to 74.1%. This suggests that future actions that would otherwise be discarded during replanning may act as noise.

### Verifying latent states with a world model (Appendices E and F)
Instead of scoring actions directly with $V_{\text{act}}$, the authors tested $V_{\text{latent}}$, which predicts and evaluates latent features 10 steps ahead using a world model. As shown in Figures F5 and F6, the world-model-based verifier demonstrated higher robustness and success rates in perturbed LIBERO-plus environments.

### Why does TTC fail to re-amplify on the 20k checkpoint? (Appendices J and K)
For heavily trained models (20k), single-candidate performance improves through distillation, but subsequent TTC provides virtually no additional boost. Measuring the cosine similarity of improvement vectors across 32 candidate generations in identical states revealed a drop from 0.22 at 5k/10k down to 0.13 at 20k. Geometrically, as the model matures, differences between candidates become so subtle that the verifier's indicated direction of improvement fluctuates wildly between samplings.

captions.F5: Comparison of Agg-8 success rates across all 420 tasks in LIBERO-plus. The x-axis represents direct action evaluation ($V_{\text{act}}$), while the y-axis represents world-model latent evaluation ($V_{\text{latent}}$). Most points sit above the diagonal, showing the benefit of world-model evaluation, especially on Object tasks.
captions.F6: Comparison of verifier input representations using the SmolVLA 4k checkpoint. Compared to the baseline and action-evaluating $V_{\text{act}}$, $V_{\text{latent}}$ (green)—which predicts and scores SmolVLA's own features via a world model—achieves the highest success rate.

takeaways: Compute spent on test-time compute (TTC) does not have to be thrown away; collecting successful rollouts and distilling them into LoRA retains gains permanently for future single-candidate inference.
Without reinforcement learning loops, simply imitating verifier-aggregated actions using flow matching provides exceptionally high sample efficiency for policy adaptation.

While early-stage checkpoints (5k) achieve both single-candidate improvements and subsequent TTC re-amplification, mature models have narrower candidate diversity, leading to saturation in TTC synergy.
Masking distillation loss to only the initial steps actually executed and verified in the environment can yield even higher adaptation performance than training on entire planned chunks.
limitations: Adaptation requires at least one successful task completion, meaning it cannot initiate under severe distribution shifts where the success rate drops to zero.
The system relies entirely on the discriminative accuracy of an offline pre-trained verifier, which itself cannot adapt to unseen environmental shifts.
The method assumes task-specific LoRA parameters updated independently, leaving cross-task knowledge sharing and multi-task adaptation unaddressed.
Evaluations are limited to simulation (LIBERO), leaving real-robot latency and detector errors unassessed.
